question: How do I hire a fractional CRO for a consumer app business?
body:
## Direct Answer
To hire a fractional CRO for a consumer app business, define the specific revenue problem you need solved (activation, monetization, retention, or paid-acquisition efficiency), then recruit an operator who has scaled consumer subscription or in-app-purchase revenue at your stage — not an enterprise B2B sales leader. Scope the engagement to two or three days a week, tie compensation to a small base retainer plus equity or a milestone bonus, and run a 60-to-90-day trial before committing to a longer term.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer for a consumer app is a different exercise than hiring one for B2B SaaS, because your "revenue engine" is not a sales team — it is a funnel of installs, onboarding, paywalls, notifications, and lifecycle marketing. The right fractional CRO for you is a growth-and-monetization operator who can read cohort curves and app-store economics, not a quota-carrying deal closer. This guide walks through when the role makes sense, how to scope it, what to pay, how to source candidates, and how to structure the first 90 days so the arrangement actually moves LTV, retention, and payback period.

## What does a fractional CRO actually own in a consumer app company?
In a consumer app business, revenue does not arrive through signed contracts and pipeline reviews — it arrives through millions of small decisions users make about whether to install, activate, subscribe, and stay. A fractional CRO in this context owns the end-to-end monetization system: the pricing and packaging of subscriptions or in-app purchases, the conversion path from free to paid, the retention and win-back loops that determine lifetime value, and the efficiency of paid acquisition measured against that lifetime value. They sit above the growth, product-marketing, and lifecycle functions and make the whole thing add up to a healthy unit-economic picture.

That ownership is broader than a "head of growth" and narrower than a full commercial CEO. A fractional CRO is accountable for the revenue number and the levers underneath it, but they are doing it part-time — typically two to three days a week — which means they must be senior enough to diagnose fast, prioritize ruthlessly, and delegate execution to your existing team. The best ones spend their limited hours on the few decisions that compound: fixing a leaky paywall, reworking the onboarding that gates activation, or reallocating spend away from channels that never pay back. If you find yourself wanting someone to sit in the tool all day building campaigns, you want a full-time growth hire, not a fractional executive. For a deeper look at how this role differs from a VP of Sales, see our breakdown at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-vs-vp-sales.

![How do I hire a fractional CRO for a consumer app business — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9079-b1.jpg)


The distinction matters because mis-hiring here is expensive. A classic failure mode is bringing on a decorated B2B enterprise CRO who has never seen an app-store console, does not know what a D30 retention curve should look like, and tries to install a pipeline-and-forecast operating rhythm onto a business that has no salespeople. The revenue mechanics of consumer are genuinely different, and the fractional executive you hire has to have lived inside them.

## When should a consumer app hire a fractional CRO instead of a full-time one?
The fractional model fits a specific window. Below roughly one to two million dollars in annual recurring or annualized app revenue, most consumer app teams cannot yet justify — or afford — a full-time revenue executive, but they have grown past the point where the founder can hold monetization, growth, and lifecycle in their own head. That gap is exactly where a fractional CRO earns their fee: senior judgment applied to the highest-leverage problems, without the fully loaded cost of a full-time C-level hire and equity grant.

![How do I hire a fractional CRO for a consumer app business — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9079-b2.jpg)


There are three signals that you are in the window. First, your growth has plateaued and you cannot tell whether the problem is acquisition, activation, or retention — you need someone who can read the funnel and name the constraint. Second, you are spending on paid user acquisition but are not confident the spend pays back inside an acceptable window, and no one owns the LTV-to-CAC relationship end to end. Third, you have product-market fit signals but your monetization feels accidental — the paywall was built once and never touched, pricing has never been tested, and no one is systematically improving conversion. Any one of these justifies the conversation; two or three make it urgent.

You should hire full-time instead of fractional when revenue is large enough that a few points of improvement dwarf the executive's salary, when the role requires daily presence to manage a growing team, or when you are raising a round where investors expect a full-time commercial leader in the seat. Many companies use the fractional arrangement as an explicit bridge: a fractional CRO stabilizes the revenue engine, builds the operating rhythm, and helps recruit their own full-time successor. That succession-planning framing is often the healthiest way to enter the engagement, and we cover the transition mechanics at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-to-fulltime-transition.

![How do I hire a fractional CRO for a consumer app business — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9079-b3.jpg)


```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Revenue plateau or unclear funnel] --> B{Annualized app revenue}
  B -->|Under 1 to 2 million| C[Fractional CRO fits]
  B -->|Over 3 to 5 million| D[Move toward full time CRO]
  C --> E{Is the core problem clear}
  E -->|No diagnose first| F[Two to three day per week engagement]
  E -->|Yes execute now| G[Milestone based scope]
  F --> H[Sixty to ninety day trial]
  G --> H
  H --> I{Did key metric move}
  I -->|Yes| J[Extend or transition to full time]
  I -->|No| K[Exit cleanly and reassess]
```

## What specific experience should a consumer app fractional CRO have?
The single most important filter is category fit. A consumer app fractional CRO should have personally scaled revenue in a business that monetizes the way yours does. If you run a subscription app, they should have grown subscription revenue and know the difference between trial-start optimization and trial-conversion optimization. If you monetize through in-app purchases or a freemium consumable model, they should understand whales, payer conversion, and the economics of virtual goods. If you rely on advertising revenue, they should understand eCPMs, fill rate, and mediation. These are not interchangeable skill sets, and a candidate who has only done one may quietly assume it applies everywhere.

Beyond monetization model, look for fluency in the platform realities that shape consumer revenue. That means real experience with app-store economics — the platform commission on subscriptions, the mechanics of store optimization, and the measurement constraints introduced by privacy changes that broke deterministic attribution. A candidate who cannot discuss how they navigated the shift to probabilistic and modeled attribution has not been operating in consumer recently enough. They should also be comfortable with cohort analysis as a native language: reading retention curves, understanding why a flattening D30 curve matters more than a spiky D1, and translating those curves into lifetime-value forecasts that drive spend decisions.

Finally, weigh the operating-stage match. Someone who scaled a consumer app from ten million to a hundred million in revenue is impressive but may be the wrong hire if you are trying to get from one million to five — the problems, and the instincts, are different. At your stage the constraint is usually finding the first repeatable monetization and retention wins, not optimizing a mature machine. Ask candidates to describe the last time they took a business at your exact stage and named the one constraint that unlocked growth. The specificity of that answer tells you whether they will diagnose your business or pattern-match a playbook that does not fit. For a framework on evaluating operator-stage fit, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/operator-stage-fit.

## How should I structure the compensation and contract?
Consumer app fractional CRO compensation typically combines three components: a monthly retainer for the committed days, an equity grant vested over the engagement, and sometimes a performance bonus tied to a specific metric. The retainer reflects the day commitment and the executive's seniority; a two-to-three-day-a-week arrangement is priced well below a full-time salary precisely because it is fractional. Do not fabricate a market number in your own head — get two or three real quotes from candidates and let the market tell you the range, because it varies widely by the operator's track record and your stage.

The equity component is where consumer arrangements often go wrong. Because the engagement is part-time and may last only six to twelve months, the grant should be smaller than a full-time executive hire and should vest on a schedule that matches the actual commitment — often monthly over the engagement term with a short cliff, rather than the standard four-year full-time vest. Tie a portion to staying through a defined milestone so incentives align with the outcome you actually care about. If you attach a performance bonus, anchor it to a metric the CRO can genuinely influence within the engagement window, such as improving trial-to-paid conversion or reducing blended CAC payback, rather than to top-line revenue that depends on factors outside their control.

Structure the contract itself as a short initial term with a clear exit. A 60-to-90-day trial with a defined success metric protects both sides: you learn whether the fit is real before committing to a year, and the CRO gets a fair window to show impact. Put the scope, the days, the metric, the reporting cadence, and the termination terms in writing. Ambiguity about what "success" means is the most common reason these engagements sour, and a one-page scope document up front prevents most of it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Base retainer for committed days] --> D[Total package]
  B[Equity vesting over engagement] --> D
  C[Milestone bonus on one metric] --> D
  D --> E{Sixty to ninety day trial}
  E -->|Metric moved| F[Extend term and expand scope]
  E -->|Metric flat| G[Clean exit per contract terms]
```

## How do I run the first 90 days so the engagement actually works?
The first two weeks should be pure diagnosis. A good fractional CRO will pull your cohort data, your funnel from install to paid, your channel-level acquisition economics, and your pricing and paywall history, then come back with a written diagnosis of the single biggest constraint on revenue. Resist the urge to have them start "executing" on day one. The entire value of a senior operator is that they name the right problem before spending your money and their limited hours on it. If a candidate wants to launch tactics before they have read your cohorts, that is a warning sign.

Weeks three through eight are about landing one or two visible wins that build organizational trust and prove the thesis. This is deliberate: a fractional executive has no positional authority and limited hours, so early credibility is what unlocks the harder, slower work later. Common early wins in consumer apps include reworking a paywall that has never been tested, fixing an onboarding step that is silently killing activation, or cutting spend on a channel that has never paid back and redeploying it. Each of these can move a real metric inside the trial window, which is exactly what you want to see before extending.

By the end of the first 90 days you should have three things: a clear read on whether the key metric moved, an operating rhythm the team can sustain, and a decision about the path forward. That path is usually one of three — extend the fractional engagement into a longer term, begin transitioning toward a full-time CRO the fractional operator helps recruit, or exit cleanly because the fit or the impact was not there. Deciding this explicitly, against the metric you defined at the start, is what separates a disciplined engagement from an open-ended consulting spend that quietly renews forever. For the reporting cadence and dashboard we recommend during this window, see our operating-rhythm guide referenced throughout the PULSE knowledge base.

## What are the biggest mistakes companies make hiring a fractional CRO for a consumer app?
The most common mistake is hiring for the wrong monetization model. A founder reads an impressive resume, sees "CRO" and "scaled revenue," and hires someone whose entire career was enterprise B2B sales. That person has genuine skill, but it is skill in building pipeline and closing deals — neither of which exists in a consumer app. They will be lost inside your cohort curves and app-store console, and the mismatch usually surfaces two months in, after you have paid a retainer and lost a quarter. Screen hard for consumer-specific, monetization-model-specific experience before anything else.

The second mistake is scope ambiguity. Because the role is senior and part-time, it is tempting to hire someone "to own revenue" without defining what that means in your business this quarter. The result is a highly paid operator who spreads thin across everything and moves nothing decisively. Define the one or two metrics that matter, put them in the contract, and let the CRO concentrate their limited hours there. A fractional executive with a sharp mandate outperforms a full-time one with a vague one.

The third mistake is treating the engagement as permanent by default. The fractional model works best when it has a defined purpose and a defined end state — stabilize monetization, build the rhythm, and either extend deliberately or transition to full-time. Engagements that quietly renew month after month without a metric check tend to drift into expensive advisory relationships that no longer create leverage. Set the 60-to-90-day checkpoint, hold it honestly, and make an active decision each time. That discipline is what keeps a fractional CRO an asset rather than a line item.

## Related questions
### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a growth consultant?
A fractional CRO owns the revenue number and the team executing against it as an accountable part-time executive, while a growth consultant advises and hands off recommendations without owning the outcome or the people.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO typically work?
Most consumer app fractional CRO engagements run two to three days per week, enough for senior diagnosis and prioritization while keeping the cost well below a full-time executive hire.

### Can a fractional CRO help me raise a funding round?
Yes — a fractional CRO can sharpen your unit economics, build a defensible LTV-to-CAC story, and prepare the revenue narrative investors scrutinize, though investors often expect a full-time commercial leader before a larger round.

### Should a seed-stage consumer app hire a fractional CRO?
Usually not until there are product-market-fit signals and some paid revenue; before that the founder should own monetization directly, because there is not yet enough of a funnel for a revenue executive to optimize.

### How do I measure whether my fractional CRO is working?
Define one or two metrics up front — such as trial-to-paid conversion or CAC payback — and check them against a 60-to-90-day baseline, rather than judging by activity or top-line revenue alone.

## FAQ
**What does a fractional CRO cost for a consumer app?**
Cost is structured as a monthly retainer for the committed days plus a small equity grant, and sometimes a milestone bonus. The retainer scales with the operator's track record and your stage, so get real quotes from two or three candidates rather than assuming a fixed market rate.

**How is a consumer app CRO different from a B2B SaaS CRO?**
A B2B CRO manages a sales team, pipeline, and forecast. A consumer app CRO manages a funnel of installs, activation, paywalls, retention loops, and paid-acquisition efficiency. The core skill is reading cohort and unit economics, not closing deals, so the two roles are not interchangeable.

**How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?**
Start with a 60-to-90-day trial tied to a defined metric. From there, engagements commonly run six to twelve months, ending either in a deliberate extension or a transition to a full-time hire the fractional operator helps recruit.

**What metrics will a fractional CRO focus on first?**
Typically the constraint metric — the single biggest limiter on revenue. In consumer apps that is often activation rate, trial-to-paid conversion, D30 retention, or CAC payback period, depending on where the funnel is leaking.

**Should I give a fractional CRO equity?**
Usually yes, but a smaller grant than a full-time executive, vesting over the actual engagement term rather than a standard four-year full-time schedule. Tie a portion to a defined milestone so incentives match the outcome you care about.

**Where do I find qualified fractional CRO candidates for consumer apps?**
Sources include operator and fractional-executive networks, warm introductions from other consumer app founders, investors who have seen many revenue leaders, and specialized talent marketplaces. Prioritize referrals from founders whose apps monetize the way yours does.

**Can a fractional CRO also manage my paid acquisition spend?**
They should own the strategy and the LTV-to-CAC discipline behind the spend, but day-to-day campaign execution is usually better left to a growth manager or agency. The fractional CRO sets the guardrails and reallocates budget; they should not be building ad sets themselves.

**How do I transition from a fractional to a full-time CRO?**
Have the fractional CRO define the full-time role, help source and interview candidates, and overlap briefly to hand off the operating rhythm and context. Planning this succession from the start is often the healthiest framing for the engagement.
